newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: France pledges crackdown on French Guiana violence.
newsitem.headline: France pledges crackdown on French Guiana violence.

text.p: France pledged on Tuesday to crack down on violence in its South American territory of French Guiana after rioters set fire to the main police station in the capital, Cayenne.

"This violent attack using Molotov cocktails resulted in the (police) headquarters catching fire and endangered the lives of the police and Cayenne's firemen, who were hampered when they attempted to intercede," Dominique Vian, the French government representative, or prefect, told a news conference.
"I am giving a serious warning to those who irresponsibly spread false rumours to create or encourage a situation dangerous to public order," Vian said.

Violence broke out late on Monday when police and demonstrators clashed after an independence leader accused of attacking a policeman and placed in pretrial detention last month was not released following a judicial hearing.
Paramilitary riot police used tear gas to clear rioters from the city's centre. Demonstrators hurled rocks and firebombs. Officials said four policemen were slightly injured.

The violence was triggered by the arrest last month of Jean-Victor Castor, a leading member of French Guiana's independence movement. He is accused of violence against a policeman during a wave of riots in April in which nine policemen were injured, eight by gunfire.

April's riots, in turn, were triggered by the arrest of 10 other members of the independence movement for an attack on the residence of the French territory's state prosecutor during a first wave of riots in November 1996.
The violence has shattered French Guiana's tranquil facade and laid bare economic, political and social woes.
French Guiana is the only territory on the mainland of the Western Hemisphere that is not independent.
It lags behind mainland France in housing, education and health care. Official unemployment in the population of 150,000 exceeds 25 percent, and the economy is heavily dependent on French subsidies.
